title: D.O.A.

evidence.note: The Public Domain Review says the film is in the US public domain 'due to an error related to the renewal of the copyright.' Wikipedia says similarly that a filing error left the copyright unrenewed. Both are secondary sources. I did not open a renewal volume of the Catalog of Copyright Entries or the Copyright Office public catalog to confirm that no renewal exists, so the print is not marked verified_pd. For the registration side, the Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Parts 12-13, Motion Pictures and Filmstrips, Jan-Dec 1950 is on archive.org as catalogofcopyri341213libr. For the renewal side, a 1950 film's renewal window ran through 1977 and 1978. The Catalog of Copyright Entries, Fourth Series, Part 8, Renewals, Jan-June 1978 is on archive.org as catalogofcopyrig18libr. I did not locate the Jul-Dec 1978 renewal volume or the 1977 renewal volumes on archive.org, so those still need to be found and searched.

Wikipedia credits the music to Dimitri Tiomkin. I did not check whether the score was separately registered or renewed. A sound film's recorded track normally shares the film's own status, but that is unconfirmed here.

Wikipedia credits the screenplay to Russell Rouse and Clarence Greene and mentions no earlier source work. I did not confirm the absence of an underlying published work or check the screenplay's own registration or renewal, so the story layer is unresolved.

editorial:
D.O.A. is a 1950 film noir directed by Rudolph Maté, who had been nominated for the Academy Award for Best Cinematography five years in a row in the 1940s. A poisoned man walks into a police station to report his own murder, and the opening is a long tracking shot down the station corridor. Harry Popkin Productions and Cardinal Pictures made it, and United Artists distributed it.

The Public Domain Review says the film is in the US public domain because of an error in renewing its copyright. That is a secondary claim. This dossier did not check the renewal records themselves, so the print stays undetermined until someone searches the 1977 and 1978 renewal records of the Catalog of Copyright Entries and the Copyright Office public records. The rights trap is the layers beyond the picture. Dimitri Tiomkin's score and the Rouse and Greene screenplay were not checked and may carry their own registrations. D.O.A. has also been remade several times, and any remake or modern re-release adds its own protected material.
faq: The Public Domain Review says its copyright lapsed through a renewal error. This dossier could not confirm that in the primary renewal records. Search the 1977 and 1978 renewal records of the Catalog of Copyright Entries and the US Copyright Office public records yourself before relying on it. Check the music and the story separately. Do not use the later remakes.
Where can I watch or download a copy?

The Internet Archive has an item at https://archive.org/details/DOA1950, about 83 minutes long. Its description field reads only 'NA', so the print's source and quality are unverified. Any version with added titles, a new score or other new material may carry protection for those additions.
